components.text: Water moves continuously between the oceans, the atmosphere, and the land. In this lesson you will learn the three main stages and work through one example.
The Sun heats water at the surface of oceans, lakes, and rivers. Some molecules gain enough energy to escape as water vapour into the air.
As warm, moist air rises it cools. Water vapour condenses onto tiny dust particles to form clouds. When droplets grow heavy enough, they fall as precipitation.
Precipitation collects in rivers, lakes, groundwater, and oceans. Water that soaks into the ground can be taken up by plants and released again through transpiration.

items.label: Start
items.text: A shallow pond holds 10 L of water in the sun.

items.label: Evaporation
items.text: Heat turns 4 L into vapour, which rises into the air.

items.label: Condensation
items.text: The vapour cools and forms a cloud. Later, 4 L falls as rain onto a river.

items.label: Collection
items.text: The river carries that water downstream to the sea, completing the cycle.

questions.question: What drives evaporation?
questions.explanation: The Sun's heat gives water molecules enough energy to become vapour.

questions.question: How do clouds form?
options: Water vapour freezes on the ground
Water vapour cools and condenses onto particles
Rain is pushed up into the sky
questions.explanation: Rising air cools, and the vapour condenses onto dust particles to form droplets.

questions.question: Which process returns water from plants to the atmosphere?
questions.explanation: Transpiration is the release of water vapour through plant leaves.
